svg.text: Team presentation • Xiaomi T12 + Kinect v1 (assumed) + two IMUs + dual arms • Design proposal 0.2
Read top to bottom. This explains the system; connector pin numbers and several hardware choices still need verification.
The robot battery and the charging-station battery are separate. Each has its own matching battery protection and charging settings.
BMS = battery protection, not a charger. All charging returns must use the correct BMS port. T12 charging remains separate below.
A buck converter reduces voltage. One shared voltage supply can feed several compatible devices; every branch needs appropriate protection.
Mounted close to the pack; rating TBD
Measures robot load → I2C to ESP32
P1 Fuse → compute buck → USB-C source
5.1 V target; verify power at Pi under load
USB devices / SSD / fan included in budget
Confirm Kinect adapter voltage and polarity
Adapter supplies power; USB carries data to Pi
Independent of Pi supply; common system return
Each module must accept this voltage
Add module decoupling; verify breakout ratings
Body IMU + head IMU + sensor logic
I2C mux / ToF / INA228 logic as selected
Every power cable needs a return
Motor current must not flow through
the Pi or sensor ground wires.
P5 Fuse → actuator buck → power bus
Voltage and current depend on selected servos
Separate power wires; signals come from section 3
Heavy power switch; opens when permit is lost
Coil driver + suppression + precharge interlock: design TBD
E-stop target: stop motion; keep Pi / Kinect alive.
Arm brakes / gravity behavior must be designed too.
Not shown as ready-to-fit parts: transient protection, precharge/inrush limit, coil suppression, fuse values, cable gauges and connectors.
3 HOW THE ROBOT TALKS AND SENSES
Power labels P1–P5 refer to section 2. Data connections do not replace a device’s power supply. The ESP32 handles low-level control.
Two separate IMUs + optional ToF x4 [P4]
Channel 0: body IMU fixed to chassis
Channel 1: head IMU moves with camera
Other channels: front / rear / left / right ToF
SSD → USB or chosen PCIe HAT
Optional AI board: verify Pi interface
Pi has no general analog input
Left arm / right arm / grippers / pan-tilt
Signal wires from the selected driver → actuators
Motor power from P5 → separate distribution
Servo voltage, stall current and pinouts still TBD
Camera IMU is a sensor, not a pan/tilt controller
I2C = short sensor-data bus. Use correct pull-ups and local capacitors; confirm interrupt/reset wires and cable lengths after module selection.
4 THE XIAOMI BASE: KEEP ITS POWER SEPARATE FOR THE FIRST PROTOTYPE
This is a differential-drive vacuum base, not mecanum. Do not assume the existing controller exposes an open motor or LiDAR interface.
Never parallel with the new 6S pack
OEM gyro is an additional sensor
Future single-pack option: 6S → separately fused, validated base supply + motion disconnect → T12. Do not build from voltage alone.
Check battery-sense pins, peak motor current and braking energy first. Opening the new pack contactor does NOT stop an OEM-battery-powered base.
5 WHAT THE TEAM SHOULD UNDERSTAND BEFORE BUILDING
A custom PCB is optional for the prototype. Start with protected modules and a labelled wiring harness; consolidate after interfaces are proven.
The small parts do important jobs
Fuse: protects a wire branch against excess current.
Buck: reduces voltage; it does not create extra energy.
Shunt: small resistor used to measure current.
BMS: monitors/protects cells and pack temperature.
USB-C source must support the Pi’s power needs.
Do not power actuators through a sensor board.
No raw 6S into T12, Pi, ESP32 or ordinary servos.
Six 2.7 V supercaps are NOT suitable across 6S.
Standalone emergency beacon needs its own protected
battery/charger; it is optional, not a shared power rail.
Still needed to finish the wiring
Exact Kinect / adapter and T12 model labels.
Arm / gripper / pan-tilt actuator models and counts.
IMU / ToF boards, audio, storage and cooling choices.
Peak-current measurements and base API discovery.
Then: actual pin numbers, fuses, wires and PCB layout.
Runtime is a target, not a measurement: 266 Wh × 80% usable × 87% efficiency gives ~6.6 h at 28 W, or ~3.1 h at 60 W.
